title: Merchant of Record vs payment processor
description: Understand who is the legal seller, which responsibilities move, and why the fee comparison is not one-to-one.
dek: The most important payments question is not whose checkout looks best. It is whose name is on the sale and who remains responsible after the payment succeeds.
takeaways: A processor helps move money while your business normally remains the seller.
An MoR becomes the seller for eligible covered transactions and assumes the documented transaction obligations.
The fee comparison is not one-to-one because the two models purchase different operating scopes.
decisionChecklist: Confirm the legal seller shown in terms, invoices, receipts, and statements.
List the indirect-tax, fraud, dispute, and transaction-support tasks each contract covers.
Price the operating work that remains with your team.
Check product, seller-country, buyer-country, and channel eligibility.
Review data, token, and subscription portability before signing.

sections.heading: A processor moves money
body: A payment processor or payment service provider helps your business accept a card, wallet, bank debit, or transfer. Your business normally remains the seller to the customer, so your terms, invoices, refund obligations, indirect-tax registrations, filings, and product support remain yours.
Tax calculation software can reduce manual work without changing that legal relationship. A processor offering tax calculation is not automatically a Merchant of Record.

sections.heading: An MoR becomes the seller
body: A Merchant of Record buys or licenses the eligible product from you and resells it to the customer. It appears in the buyer-facing transaction and assumes the documented transaction responsibilities, commonly including indirect-tax calculation, registration, filing, remittance, fraud, disputes, and billing support.
The exact boundary is contractual. Product delivery, product support, bookkeeping, income tax, privacy obligations, and unsupported markets can remain with you.

sections.heading: The fees buy different things
body: A processor's headline rate usually prices payment acceptance. An MoR's rate usually bundles a broader operating role. A useful comparison shows the processing fee, add-ons, international and FX costs, refund and dispute behavior, payout costs, and the work your team still performs.
Do not invent a dollar value for legal, accounting, or staffing work. Add your known costs and keep unknowns visible.

sections.heading: A practical decision rule
body: Choose an MoR when eligible global digital sales, indirect-tax operations, and transaction support would otherwise slow the business more than the fee and control tradeoffs. Remain the merchant when control, product breadth, checkout flexibility, direct customer ownership, or scale economics matter more and you can operate the retained responsibilities.
